claims.source: Immunohistochemistry on E10.5 tissue sections revealed placodal neurons (Islet1-positive and Six1-positive nuclei) and undifferentiated neural crest cells (Sox10-positive nuclei) present in similar ratios throughout the forming trigeminal ganglion (Figure 2E–J).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: There is no change in the size or length of the exclusively placode-derived geniculate ganglion or chorda tympani nerve at E10.5 between Control and Elp1 CKO.
claims.source: There was also no change in the size or length of the exclusively placode-derived geniculate ganglion (387 µm Control, n=3, versus 361 µm Elp1 CKO, n=3, p=0.4559, unpaired t-test, Holm-Sidak adjustment for multiple comparisons) or chorda tympani nerve (692 µm Control, n=3, versus 686.3 µm Elp1 CKO, n=3, p=0.7671, unpaired t-test, Holm-Sidak adjustment for multiple comparisons), whose neurons are not targeted by Wnt1-Cre for Elp1 deletion (Figure 2B and C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry and quantification.

claims.claim: Elp1 is not required in neural crest cells for them to coalesce with placodal neurons as the trigeminal ganglion is initially forming.
claims.source: Altogether, these data suggest Elp1 is not required in neural crest cells for them to coalesce with placodal neurons as the trigeminal ganglion is initially forming.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that trigeminal ganglion formation appears normal at E10.5 in Elp1 CKO.

claims.claim: By E11.5, Control and Elp1 CKO display robust outgrowth of axons from the trigeminal ganglion.
claims.source: By E11.5, Control and Elp1 CKO displayed robust outgrowth of axons from the trigeminal ganglion, which contains both neural crest- and placode-derived neurons at this stage (Figure 3B and E).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: At E11.5, nerves in Elp1 CKO appeared less organized than in Controls.
claims.source: Although the ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular nerves were present and distinct in Control and Elp1 CKO, nerves in the latter appeared less organized.
claims.evidence: Observed from whole-mount immunohistochemistry images.

claims.claim: In the maxillary nerve at E11.5, Elp1 CKO axons often strayed from established bundles into the surrounding mesenchyme or crossed to adjacent fascicles.
claims.source: In the maxillary nerve, Elp1 CKO axons often strayed from established bundles into the surrounding mesenchyme or crossed to adjacent fascicles (Figure 3C and F).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Axons of the mandibular nerve in Elp1 CKO at E11.5 traveled away from the established nerve without direction, compared to the compact mandibular nerve observed in Controls.
claims.source: Axons of the mandibular nerve in Elp1 CKO also traveled away from the established nerve without direction, compared to the compact mandibular nerve observed in Controls (Figure 3D and G).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The Elp1 CKO phenotype is highly penetrant, with disrupted axon trajectories noted to varying degrees in all Elp1 CKO embryos examined.
claims.source: The Elp1 CKO phenotype is highly penetrant, and disrupted axon trajectories were noted to varying degrees in all Elp1 CKO embryos examined.
claims.evidence: Observation across multiple Elp1 CKO embryos.

claims.claim: The placode-derived chorda tympani nerve exhibited normal axon trajectories in both Control and Elp1 CKO embryos at E11.5.
claims.source: In contrast, the placode-derived chorda tympani nerve exhibited normal axon trajectories in both Control and Elp1 CKO embryos at E11.5 (Figure 3B and E).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: At E11.5, there is no significant difference in the size of the trigeminal ganglion between Control and Elp1 CKO.
claims.source: At this stage, there was no significant difference in the size of the trigeminal ganglion or the width of the central nerve root, which contains axons projecting from the trigeminal ganglion into the hindbrain, in Control versus Elp1 CKO (Figure 3H and I).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: At E11.5, there is no significant difference in the width of the central nerve root between Control and Elp1 CKO.
claims.source: At this stage, there was no significant difference in the size of the trigeminal ganglion or the width of the central nerve root, which contains axons projecting from the trigeminal ganglion into the hindbrain, in Control versus Elp1 CKO (Figure 3H and I).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: At E11.5, there are similar ratios of Sox10-positive cells and Six1-positive cells in Control and Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia.
claims.source: Additionally, there were similar ratios of Sox10-positive cells (Control = 47.1%, n=3, versus Elp1 CKO = 50.3%, n=3, of all DAPI-stained nuclei, p=0.6444, nested two-tailed t-test) and Six1-positive cells (Control = 69.7%, n=3, versus Elp1 CKO = 65.9%, n=3, of all DAPI-stained nuclei, p=0.4897, nested t-test) in Control and Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: By E12.5, trigeminal ganglion and nerve morphology were drastically altered in Elp1 CKO.
claims.source: By E12.5, trigeminal ganglion and nerve morphology were drastically altered in Elp1 CKO, with nuanced changes in specific nerve branches (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The size of the trigeminal ganglion at E12.5 trended smaller in Elp1 CKO but was not statistically significant.
claims.source: The size of the trigeminal ganglion proper trended smaller but was not statistically significant (Figure 4B, E and H).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The diameter of the nerve root at E12.5 was significantly smaller in Elp1 CKO compared to Control.
claims.source: Interestingly, the diameter of the nerve root was significantly smaller in Elp1 CKO, indicating the loss of some centrally projecting axons between E11.5 and E12.5 (Figure 4B, E and I).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The loss of centrally projecting axons occurs between E11.5 and E12.5 in Elp1 CKO.
claims.source: Interestingly, the diameter of the nerve root was significantly smaller in Elp1 CKO, indicating the loss of some centrally projecting axons between E11.5 and E12.5 (Figure 4B, E and I).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that the central root diameter is normal at E11.5 but significantly smaller at E12.5.

claims.claim: The branching complexity of the frontal nerve at E12.5 is decreased in Elp1 CKO compared to Control.
claims.source: The developing frontal nerve (ophthalmic division) was present in both Control and Elp1 CKO; however, the branching complexity of the nerve was decreased in Elp1 CKO, as quantified by a modified Sholl analysis (Figure 4C, F, J, and K, Sholl, 1953).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by modified Sholl analysis shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Stray frontal nerve axons are observed proximal to the ganglion in Elp1 CKO at E12.5.
claims.source: Stray frontal nerve axons were also observed proximal to the ganglion (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The medial and lateral nasal nerves are absent in Elp1 CKO at E12.5.
claims.source: While the ophthalmic nerve extended rostrally in both Control and Elp1 CKO, the medial and lateral nasal nerves that descend from this branch toward the nose were absent in Elp1 CKO (Figure 4D and G).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The terminal extent of the infraorbital nerve at E12.5 is smaller in Elp1 CKO compared to Control.
claims.source: The maxillary division was also impacted, such that the terminal extent of the infraorbital nerve, which innervates the whisker pad, was smaller in Elp1 CKO compared to Control (Figure 4D, G and L).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Nerve defects caused by loss of Elp1 can differ within the same ganglion, based on neuronal identity and/or specific target region.
claims.source: Together, these results provide a dynamic summary of the requirements for Elp1 in axonal pathfinding and target innervation in trigeminal ganglion sensory neurons. Importantly, our data suggest that nerve defects caused by loss of Elp1 can differ, even within the same ganglion, based on neuronal identity and/or specific target region.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that different nerve branches show distinct phenotypes in Elp1 CKO.

claims.claim: TrkA expression at E13 is strong throughout the trigeminal ganglion and along all three major nerve divisions in Control embryos.
claims.source: In Control embryos, TrkA expression was strong throughout the trigeminal ganglion and along all three major nerve divisions, detectable into the most distal branches of the frontal and infraorbital nerves (Figure 5A, B, E, and F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: TrkA immunoreactivity at E13 is drastically reduced in the central nerve root and in distal branches of the frontal nerve, the rostral ophthalmic nerve, and the infraorbital nerve in Elp1 CKO.
claims.source: In Elp1 CKO, TrkA immunoreactivity was drastically reduced in the central nerve root (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,D) and in distal branches of the frontal nerve, the rostral ophthalmic nerve, and the infraorbital nerve (Figure 5C, D, G, and H), indicating effects on both central and peripheral trigeminal projections.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: TrkA immunofluorescence at E12.5 is significantly reduced in Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia compared to Control.
claims.source: Examination of E12.5 tissue sections through the maxillary lobe revealed significantly reduced TrkA immunofluorescence in Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia compared to Control, with no change in TrkB or TrkC immunofluorescence (Figure 5I–L and Q and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-L).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: There is no change in TrkB or TrkC immunofluorescence at E12.5 in Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia compared to Control.
claims.source: Examination of E12.5 tissue sections through the maxillary lobe revealed significantly reduced TrkA immunofluorescence in Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia compared to Control, with no change in TrkB or TrkC immunofluorescence (Figure 5I–L and Q and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-L).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: There are fewer TrkA-expressing nerve endings in the upper lip at E12.5 in Elp1 CKO compared to Control.
claims.source: Sections through the upper lip, which is heavily innervated by the infraorbital nerve, demonstrated fewer TrkA-expressing nerve endings in Elp1 CKO compared to Control, while TrkC-expressing nerve endings were maintained (Figure 5M–P).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: TrkC-expressing nerve endings in the upper lip are maintained at E12.5 in Elp1 CKO.
claims.source: Sections through the upper lip, which is heavily innervated by the infraorbital nerve, demonstrated fewer TrkA-expressing nerve endings in Elp1 CKO compared to Control, while TrkC-expressing nerve endings were maintained (Figure 5M–P).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: TrkA neurons are reduced by 23% in Elp1 CKO compared to Controls at E12.5.
claims.source: While no differences were observed in the number of TrkB or TrkC neurons, TrkA neurons were reduced by 23% in Elp1 CKO compared to Controls (Figure 5R).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: There are no differences in the number of TrkB or TrkC neurons at E12.5 between Control and Elp1 CKO.
claims.source: While no differences were observed in the number of TrkB or TrkC neurons, TrkA neurons were reduced by 23% in Elp1 CKO compared to Controls (Figure 5R).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Early target innervation defects in Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglion neurons are associated with a specific loss of TrkA-expressing neurons in the ganglion and nerves.
claims.source: Therefore, early target innervation defects in Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglion neurons are associated with a specific loss of TrkA-expressing neurons in the ganglion and nerves.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that TrkA neurons are reduced and TrkA expression is decreased in nerves.

claims.claim: Most TrkA neurons in Elp1 CKO at E12.5 are devoid of Elp1 protein.
claims.source: Immunohistochemistry on E12.5 tissue sections revealed Elp1 protein expression throughout the Control trigeminal ganglion in TrkA, TrkB, and TrkC neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-C,G-I,M-O). In contrast, most TrkA neurons in Elp1 CKO were devoid of Elp1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D-F), while the majority of remaining Elp1-positive neurons expressed TrkB or TrkC (Figure 5—figure supplement 2J-L,P-R).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The majority of remaining Elp1-positive neurons in Elp1 CKO at E12.5 express TrkB or TrkC.
claims.source: Immunohistochemistry on E12.5 tissue sections revealed Elp1 protein expression throughout the Control trigeminal ganglion in TrkA, TrkB, and TrkC neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-C,G-I,M-O). In contrast, most TrkA neurons in Elp1 CKO were devoid of Elp1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D-F), while the majority of remaining Elp1-positive neurons expressed TrkB or TrkC (Figure 5—figure supplement 2J-L,P-R).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: TrkB and TrkC neurons are born first in the trigeminal ganglion followed by TrkA neurons.
claims.source: Consistent with reports that TrkB and TrkC neurons are born first in the trigeminal ganglion followed by TrkA neurons (Huang et al., 1999a; Huang et al., 1999b), immunohistochemistry on trigeminal ganglion serial sections revealed that all three Trk subtypes are present at E11, but the majority of established infraorbital nerve endings are either TrkB- or TrkC-positive, with little contribution from TrkA-expressing axons at this stage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies and confirmed by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: At E11, all three Trk subtypes are present in the trigeminal ganglion, but the majority of established infraorbital nerve endings are either TrkB- or TrkC-positive, with little contribution from TrkA-expressing axons.
claims.source: Consistent with reports that TrkB and TrkC neurons are born first in the trigeminal ganglion followed by TrkA neurons (Huang et al., 1999a; Huang et al., 1999b), immunohistochemistry on trigeminal ganglion serial sections revealed that all three Trk subtypes are present at E11, but the majority of established infraorbital nerve endings are either TrkB- or TrkC-positive, with little contribution from TrkA-expressing axons at this stage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: By E11.5, some TrkA-positive axons have reached the whisker pad region, but the majority of infraorbital nerve endings are TrkA-negative and presumably TrkB- or TrkC-positive.
claims.source: By E11.5, some TrkA-positive axons have reached the whisker pad region, but the majority of infraorbital nerve endings are TrkA-negative and presumably TrkB- or TrkC-positive (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: At E11.5, TrkC neurons comprise the largest proportion of neurons in the trigeminal ganglion, followed closely by TrkA, and TrkB representing the smallest proportion.
claims.source: At this stage, TrkC neurons comprise the largest proportion of neurons, followed closely by TrkA, and TrkB representing the smallest proportion of trigeminal ganglion neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F-H, Huang et al., 1999a; Huang et al., 1999b).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and cited from previous studies.

claims.claim: The number of TrkB and TrkC neurons does not appear to increase between E11.5 and E12.5.
claims.source: In accordance with previous reports, the number of TrkB and TrkC neurons did not appear to increase between E11.5 and E12.5, but there was a robust increase in the number of TrkA neurons, such that TrkA neurons became the vast majority of trigeminal ganglion neurons by E12.5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I-K; Huang et al., 1999b).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and cited from previous studies.

claims.claim: There is a robust increase in the number of TrkA neurons between E11.5 and E12.5, such that TrkA neurons become the vast majority of trigeminal ganglion neurons by E12.5.
claims.source: In accordance with previous reports, the number of TrkB and TrkC neurons did not appear to increase between E11.5 and E12.5, but there was a robust increase in the number of TrkA neurons, such that TrkA neurons became the vast majority of trigeminal ganglion neurons by E12.5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I-K; Huang et al., 1999b).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and cited from previous studies.

claims.claim: At E10.5, 88.6% of TrkA neurons, 78.0% of TrkB neurons, and 91.8% of TrkC neurons express Six1.
claims.source: At E10.5, we observed that 88.6% of TrkA neurons, 78.0% of TrkB neurons, and 91.8% of TrkC neurons expressed Six1 (Figure 6A, D, G and J).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: At E11.5, 85.9% of TrkA neurons express Six1, while only 6.8% of TrkB neurons and 18.6% of TrkC neurons express Six1.
claims.source: Surprisingly, at E11.5 and E12.5, the majority of Six1-expressing cells were TrkA neurons: 85.9% of TrkA neurons expressed Six1 at E11.5, while only 6.8% of TrkB neurons and 18.6% of TrkC neurons did (Figure 6B, E, H, and J).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: At E12.5, 50.6% of TrkA neurons express Six1, while only 1.8% of TrkB neurons and 6.8% of TrkC neurons express Six1.
claims.source: Similar results were noted at E12.5, with 50.6% of TrkA neurons expressing Six1, while only 1.8% of TrkB neurons and 6.8% of TrkC neurons expressed Six1 (Figure 6C, F, I, and J).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Six1 is a marker of recently differentiated neurons in the trigeminal ganglion, rather than an exclusive marker of the placodal lineage.
claims.source: When considering the timeline of TrkA versus TrkB/TrkC neurogenesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), these data suggest Six1 is a marker of recently differentiated neurons in the trigeminal ganglion, rather than an exclusive marker of the placodal lineage.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that Six1 expression shifts from TrkB/TrkC neurons to TrkA neurons over developmental time, correlating with the timing of neurogenesis.

claims.claim: At E10.5, 92.1% of Sox10-positive neural crest cells in the trigeminal ganglion express GFP in Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG mice.
claims.source: In the Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG mouse, 92.1% of Sox10-positive neural crest cells in the trigeminal ganglion expressed GFP at E10.5, indicating a large proportion of neural crest cells are targeted for Wnt1-Cre-mediated recombination (Figure 7A–D).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: At E10.5, only 12.1% of Six1-expressing cells in the trigeminal ganglion are GFP-positive in Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG mice.
claims.source: Indeed, at E10.5, only 12.1% of Six1-expressing cells in the trigeminal ganglion were GFP-positive, confirming that the majority of Six1-positive cells are placode-derived at this stage (Figure 7E–H).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: At E12.5, 91.7% of Six1-positive cells in the trigeminal ganglion express GFP in Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG mice.
claims.source: In contrast, at E12.5, 91.7% of Six1-positive cells expressed GFP, indicating a shift to mostly neural crest-derived Six1-expressing cells at later stages of trigeminal ganglion neurogenesis (Figure 7I–L).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The majority of Six1-expressing cells at E10.5 are placode-derived.
claims.source: Indeed, at E10.5, only 12.1% of Six1-expressing cells in the trigeminal ganglion were GFP-positive, confirming that the majority of Six1-positive cells are placode-derived at this stage (Figure 7E–H).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the low percentage of Six1-positive cells that are GFP-positive (neural crest-derived) at E10.5.

claims.claim: There is a shift to mostly neural crest-derived Six1-expressing cells at later stages of trigeminal ganglion neurogenesis (E12.5).
claims.source: In contrast, at E12.5, 91.7% of Six1-positive cells expressed GFP, indicating a shift to mostly neural crest-derived Six1-expressing cells at later stages of trigeminal ganglion neurogenesis (Figure 7I–L).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the high percentage of Six1-positive cells that are GFP-positive (neural crest-derived) at E12.5.

claims.claim: At E15.5, only 24.4% of TrkA neurons express RFP (non-recombined, presumably placode-derived) in Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG mice.
claims.source: At E15.5, only 24.4% of TrkA neurons, versus 77.4% of TrkB neurons and 78.6% of TrkC neurons, expressed RFP (Figure 8E–P).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: At E15.5, 77.4% of TrkB neurons and 78.6% of TrkC neurons express RFP (non-recombined, presumably placode-derived) in Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG mice.
claims.source: At E15.5, only 24.4% of TrkA neurons, versus 77.4% of TrkB neurons and 78.6% of TrkC neurons, expressed RFP (Figure 8E–P).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Approximately three quarters of TrkA neurons in the embryonic trigeminal ganglion are neural crest-derived.
claims.source: These findings suggest that approximately three quarters of TrkA neurons in the embryonic trigeminal ganglion are neural crest-derived, while just one quarter of TrkB/C neurons are neural crest-derived.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that only 24.4% of TrkA neurons express RFP (placode-derived marker).

claims.claim: Just one quarter of TrkB/C neurons in the embryonic trigeminal ganglion are neural crest-derived.
claims.source: These findings suggest that approximately three quarters of TrkA neurons in the embryonic trigeminal ganglion are neural crest-derived, while just one quarter of TrkB/C neurons are neural crest-derived.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that approximately 77-79% of TrkB and TrkC neurons express RFP (placode-derived marker).

claims.claim: There is a strong correlation between cellular origin and eventual Trk receptor expression in the developing trigeminal ganglion.
claims.source: Thus, there is a strong correlation between cellular origin and eventual Trk receptor expression in the developing trigeminal ganglion, such that targeting neural crest cells will be more likely to affect TrkA versus TrkB or TrkC neurons, as seen in Elp1 CKO.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the lineage tracing data showing that most TrkA neurons are neural crest-derived while most TrkB/TrkC neurons are placode-derived.

claims.claim: Total TUNEL fluorescence at E12.5 is statistically higher in the Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglion compared to Control.
claims.source: At E12.5, TUNEL fluorescent puncta were distributed throughout Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia, and total TUNEL fluorescence was statistically higher in the E12.5 Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglion compared to Control, which only exhibited occasional, scattered TUNEL staining at this stage (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by TUNEL assay and quantification shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: TUNEL-positive nuclei at E12.5 are often found in TrkA-expressing cells in Elp1 CKO.
claims.source: Indeed, TUNEL-positive nuclei were often found in TrkA-expressing cells (Figure 9G and H).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by TUNEL assay and immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Glial precursors in the trigeminal ganglion phagocytose the cellular debris of nearby apoptotic sensory neurons.
claims.source: This suggests that glial precursors in the trigeminal ganglion phagocytose the cellular debris of nearby apoptotic sensory neurons, as previously reported in the trunk (Wu et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that TUNEL particles are found in glial cytoplasm but not nuclei, and cited from a previous study.

claims.claim: Apoptosis of TrkA neurons is not explained by changes in the TrkA ligand, NGF, as NGF protein distribution in trigeminal nerve target tissues is similar between Control and Elp1 CKO.
claims.source: Importantly, apoptosis of TrkA neurons was not explained by changes in the TrkA ligand, NGF, as NGF protein distribution in trigeminal nerve target tissues was similar between Control and Elp1 CKO (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Aberrant TUNEL staining is not observed in Elp1 CKO geniculate ganglia compared to Control at E12.5.
claims.source: Moreover, aberrant TUNEL staining was not observed in Elp1 CKO geniculate ganglia compared to Control at E12.5, suggesting neural crest-derived neurons are most affected by apoptosis in Elp1 CKO cranial ganglia at the examined timepoints (Figure 9—figure supplement 1E-H).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by TUNEL assay shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Neural crest-derived neurons are most affected by apoptosis in Elp1 CKO cranial ganglia at the examined timepoints.
claims.source: Moreover, aberrant TUNEL staining was not observed in Elp1 CKO geniculate ganglia compared to Control at E12.5, suggesting neural crest-derived neurons are most affected by apoptosis in Elp1 CKO cranial ganglia at the examined timepoints (Figure 9—figure supplement 1E-H).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that the placode-derived geniculate ganglion does not show increased apoptosis in Elp1 CKO.

claims.claim: Deletion of Elp1 from the neural crest lineage leads to innervation defects in the head and the selective loss of TrkA neurons as a result of widespread cell death within the trigeminal ganglion.
claims.source: Collectively, these findings suggest that deletion of Elp1 from the neural crest lineage leads to innervation defects in the head and the selective loss of TrkA neurons as a result of widespread cell death within the trigeminal ganglion.
claims.evidence: Summary inference from multiple observations including innervation defects, TrkA neuron loss, and increased apoptosis.

claims.claim: Elp1 protein expression overlaps with β-galactosidase staining in Elp1LacZ mice, but Elp1 protein is more selectively expressed in neurons.
claims.source: While the anatomical distribution of Elp1 protein overlapped with β-galactosidase staining in Elp1LacZ mice, the observation that Elp1 protein is more selectively expressed in neurons indicates Elp1 expression is potentially controlled at the post-transcriptional or post-translational level, such that Elp1 protein may be upregulated upon neuronal differentiation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the comparison of Elp1 protein and β-galactosidase expression patterns.

claims.claim: Elp1 expression may be controlled at the post-transcriptional or post-translational level, such that Elp1 protein may be upregulated upon neuronal differentiation.
claims.source: While the anatomical distribution of Elp1 protein overlapped with β-galactosidase staining in Elp1LacZ mice, the observation that Elp1 protein is more selectively expressed in neurons indicates Elp1 expression is potentially controlled at the post-transcriptional or post-translational level, such that Elp1 protein may be upregulated upon neuronal differentiation.
claims.evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed difference between Elp1 protein and β-galactosidase expression.

claims.claim: The presence of highly enriched Elp1 protein in neuronal cytoplasm, including axonal compartments, suggests there are extranuclear functions for Elp1 in trigeminal ganglion neurons.
claims.source: The presence of highly enriched Elp1 protein in neuronal cytoplasm, including axonal compartments, suggests there are extranuclear functions for Elp1 in trigeminal ganglion neurons, as noted in studies in other neuronal systems that localize Elp1 to axonal transport and synaptic vesicles (Abashidze et al., 2014; Naftelberg et al., 2016; Tourtellotte, 2016; Li et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the subcellular localization of Elp1 protein and cited from previous studies.

claims.claim: Elp1 is not required for trunk neural crest cell migration or subsequent formation of dorsal root or sympathetic ganglia.
claims.source: Although migration was not directly examined here, our findings complement conclusions that Elp1 is not required for trunk neural crest cell migration or subsequent formation of dorsal root or sympathetic ganglia (Abashidze et al., 2014; George et al., 2013; Hunnicutt et al., 2012; Jackson et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies and supported by the observation that trigeminal ganglion formation appears normal at E10.5.

claims.claim: Knockdown of Elp3 inhibits neural crest cell migration in Xenopus.
claims.source: Interestingly, knockdown of another elongator complex member, Elp3, inhibits neural crest cell migration in Xenopus, suggesting elongator subunits may have distinct individual functions in the neural crest (Yang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Cited from a previous study.

claims.claim: Elongator subunits may have distinct individual functions in the neural crest.

results.result: Elp1 protein is enriched in the cytoplasm of differentiated trigeminal ganglion neurons, including both neural crest- and placode-derived neurons, with highest expression in axons. At E10.5, Elp1 is initially expressed in placode-derived neurons, while condensed neural crest cells express little to no Elp1. By E11.5, Elp1 is observed in all differentiated neurons irrespective of developmental origin.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C48 provide immunohistochemistry data from multiple developmental timepoints (E10.5-E12.5) showing Elp1 protein localization in differentiated neurons (identified by Islet1, β-tubulin III) but not in undifferentiated neural crest cells (identified by Neuropilin 2, Pax3, Sox10). The temporal progression and cell-type specificity are well-documented with appropriate markers and imaging data (Figure 1).

results.result: Elp1 is not required for initial trigeminal ganglion formation at E10.5. Control and Elp1 CKO embryos show similar trigeminal ganglion size, nerve branch presence, nerve lengths, and ratios of placodal neurons to neural crest cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C55 provide quantitative measurements (ganglion size, nerve lengths) and immunohistochemistry data showing no significant differences between Control and Elp1 CKO at E10.5. Statistical tests (unpaired t-tests with multiple comparison adjustments) support the lack of differences. The placode-derived geniculate ganglion also shows no changes, serving as an appropriate control (C55).

results.result: By E11.5, Elp1 CKO trigeminal neurons exhibit abnormal axon outgrowth with disorganized, defasciculated axons in the maxillary and mandibular nerves, while the placode-derived chorda tympani nerve remains normal. Trigeminal ganglion size and cellular composition remain unchanged at this stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C65 provide whole-mount immunohistochemistry images and quantitative data showing axon disorganization in Elp1 CKO at E11.5 (Figure 3). The phenotype is described as highly penetrant across all examined embryos (C61). The normal appearance of the placode-derived chorda tympani nerve (C62) serves as an internal control, supporting the neural crest-specific effect.

results.result: By E12.5, trigeminal ganglion and nerve morphology are drastically altered in Elp1 CKO with context-dependent defects in different nerve branches. The central nerve root diameter is significantly reduced, frontal nerve branching complexity is decreased, nasal nerves are absent, and infraorbital nerve extent is reduced.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C73 provide detailed morphological analysis with quantitative measurements (modified Sholl analysis for branching complexity, nerve extent measurements) and whole-mount imaging (Figure 4). Statistical significance is demonstrated for central root diameter (C68) and infraorbital nerve extent (C73). The observation of distinct phenotypes in different nerve branches (C74) is well-supported by the diverse defects documented.

results.result: TrkA expression and TrkA-expressing neurons are specifically reduced in Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia and nerves at E12.5-E13, while TrkB and TrkC expression and neuron numbers remain unchanged. TrkA neurons are reduced by 23% in Elp1 CKO compared to Controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C82 provide both whole-mount and section immunohistochemistry data with quantitative measurements of TrkA, TrkB, and TrkC immunofluorescence and neuron counts (Figure 5). Statistical analysis shows significant reduction in TrkA (p=0.0037 for fluorescence, 23% reduction in neuron number) but no changes in TrkB or TrkC. The specificity of the TrkA defect is well-documented across multiple assays.

results.result: Most TrkA neurons in Elp1 CKO at E12.5 are devoid of Elp1 protein, while the majority of remaining Elp1-positive neurons express TrkB or TrkC.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are supported by immunohistochemistry data showing co-localization of Elp1 with different Trk receptors in Control and Elp1 CKO (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). This provides direct evidence that the neural crest-specific deletion of Elp1 primarily affects TrkA neurons, consistent with the lineage data.

results.result: TrkB and TrkC neurons are born first in the trigeminal ganglion followed by TrkA neurons. Six1 expression shifts from predominantly TrkB/TrkC neurons at E10.5 to predominantly TrkA neurons at E11.5-E12.5, suggesting Six1 is a marker of recently differentiated neurons rather than an exclusive marker of placodal lineage.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C94 provide detailed temporal analysis of Trk receptor expression and Six1 co-localization across multiple developmental stages (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Quantitative data show the shift in Six1 expression from TrkB/TrkC neurons (78-92% at E10.5) to TrkA neurons (86% at E11.5, 51% at E12.5). The interpretation that Six1 marks recently differentiated neurons (C95) is a reasonable inference from the temporal correlation with neurogenesis timing.

results.result: Lineage tracing using Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG mice shows that at E10.5, 92.1% of Sox10-positive neural crest cells express GFP, while only 12.1% of Six1-positive cells are GFP-positive, confirming most Six1-positive cells are placode-derived at this stage. By E12.5, 91.7% of Six1-positive cells express GFP, indicating a shift to mostly neural crest-derived Six1-expressing cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C100 provide quantitative lineage tracing data with clear percentages and appropriate controls (Figure 7). The high efficiency of Wnt1-Cre recombination in Sox10-positive cells (92.1%) validates the approach. The temporal shift in Six1-positive cell lineage from predominantly placode (87.9% at E10.5) to predominantly neural crest (91.7% at E12.5) is well-documented.

results.result: At E15.5, approximately three quarters of TrkA neurons are neural crest-derived (75.6% GFP-positive), while approximately three quarters of TrkB and TrkC neurons are placode-derived (77.4% and 78.6% RFP-positive, respectively). This demonstrates a strong correlation between cellular origin and Trk receptor expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C104 provide quantitative lineage tracing data at E15.5 using the Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG reporter (Figure 8). The percentages are clearly stated and the inverse relationship between TrkA (mostly neural crest) and TrkB/TrkC (mostly placode) is well-documented. The inference of correlation between lineage and Trk expression (C105) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia show significantly increased TUNEL staining at E12.5, with TUNEL-positive nuclei often found in TrkA-expressing cells. NGF expression in target tissues is unchanged. The placode-derived geniculate ganglion shows no increased apoptosis, suggesting neural crest-derived neurons are most affected.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 provide quantitative TUNEL data showing statistically significant increase in Elp1 CKO (p=0.0052) with co-localization to TrkA neurons (Figure 9). The observation that NGF expression is unchanged (C110, Figure 9—figure supplement 2) rules out one potential mechanism. The lack of increased apoptosis in the placode-derived geniculate ganglion (C111) serves as an appropriate control supporting the neural crest-specific effect (C112).

results.result: Elp1 protein expression is more selectively expressed in neurons compared to β-galactosidase in Elp1LacZ mice, suggesting potential post-transcriptional or post-translational regulation. The enrichment of Elp1 in neuronal cytoplasm and axons suggests extranuclear functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115 present a speculative interpretation of the difference between Elp1 protein and β-galactosidase expression patterns. While the observation is valid (C114), the proposed mechanism (C115) is explicitly speculative and alternative explanations (different protein half-lives, detection threshold differences) are mentioned but not tested. Claim C116 makes a reasonable inference about extranuclear functions based on subcellular localization, supported by citations to similar findings in other systems.

results.result: Elp1 is not required for trunk neural crest cell migration or formation of dorsal root or sympathetic ganglia, though other elongator subunits like Elp3 may have distinct functions in neural crest migration.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 is supported by citations to multiple previous studies and is consistent with the current observation that trigeminal ganglion formation appears normal at E10.5. Claims C118-C119 cite a previous study showing different effects of Elp3 knockdown, supporting the interpretation that elongator subunits may have distinct functions. However, this result is primarily based on prior work rather than new data from this manuscript.

results.result: Different trigeminal nerve branches show distinct phenotypes in Elp1 CKO: frontal nerve axons reach targets but retract, while nasal nerve axons fail to navigate to targets. This suggests context-dependent mechanisms and that Elp1 is required for axonal outgrowth and proper target innervation.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121 make reasonable inferences from the temporal imaging data showing frontal nerve branches present at E12.5 but reduced by E13 (retraction), versus nasal nerves that never form (navigation failure). The interpretation that Elp1 is required for axonal outgrowth and innervation (C122) and that multiple context-dependent mechanisms are involved (C123) are well-supported by the diverse phenotypes documented across different nerve branches.

results.result: Loss of Elp1 from neural crest cells has major effects after neuronal differentiation rather than during neurogenesis. Unlike in dorsal root ganglia where Elp1 loss affects Pax3-positive progenitors, trigeminal ganglion Pax3-positive cells express little Elp1 and are glial rather than neuronal progenitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 provide data and citations distinguishing the trigeminal ganglion from dorsal root ganglia. The observation of normal Six1-positive neuron numbers at E11.5 (C125) and low Elp1 expression in Pax3-positive cells (C126) support the interpretation that neurogenesis is not primarily affected (C128). The conclusion that Elp1 effects occur after differentiation (C129) is a reasonable inference from the temporal data, though the authors acknowledge not definitively ruling out neurogenic deficits.

results.result: While Elp1 has been reported to modulate TrkA/NGF retrograde signaling in sympathetic neurons, several observations in the trigeminal ganglion (loss of TrkA in distal axons, absence of some nerve branches, normal NGF expression) suggest additional or alternative mechanisms beyond retrograde signaling deficits.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C131 cite previous work on TrkA signaling. Claims C132-C134 present observations from the current study that are inconsistent with a simple retrograde signaling deficit model: reduced TrkA expression in axon terminals (C133), complete absence of some nerves (C134), and normal NGF in targets (C132). The authors appropriately note these contradictions and suggest the need for additional mechanisms, making this a well-reasoned critical analysis of their data.

results.result: Elp1 may function in axonal outgrowth through NGF-independent mechanisms including anterograde trafficking, local protein synthesis, axon guidance, or inter-axonal adhesion. Supporting evidence includes reduced Cadherin-7 in Elp1 CKO dorsal root ganglia and broad proteomic changes affecting axon guidance pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C136, C139, and C140 are explicitly speculative, proposing potential mechanisms without direct testing. Claims C137-C138 and C141-C143 cite previous studies showing gene expression changes, proteomic alterations, and Cadherin-7 reduction in other systems, but these are not directly demonstrated in the trigeminal ganglion in this study. While these are reasonable hypotheses for future investigation, they remain speculative in the context of the current work.

results.result: The mouse trigeminal ganglion is a mosaic of neural crest- and placode-derived neurons with no spatial segregation by lineage, unlike the chick. The Trk-expressing neuronal composition is established during mid- to late-gestation and remains constant into early postnatal life.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C148 cite previous literature establishing differences between chick and mouse trigeminal ganglion organization and the correlation between cell size and lineage. Claim C149 cites a recent study showing similar proportions of Wnt1-Cre-recombined TrkA neurons in postnatal mice. Claim C150 makes a reasonable inference from comparing the current embryonic data with the cited postnatal data, though direct longitudinal tracking was not performed.

results.result: The 22q11DS deletion mouse shows targeted effects on TrkA neurons preceded by premature neurogenic divisions of neural crest cells and increased variation of neuronal gene expression at E9.5 and E10.5.
results.evaluation: Claim C151 cites findings from a recent study (Karpinski et al., 2022) and is used to provide context for the current findings. This is appropriately cited prior work rather than a new result from this manuscript.

results.result: Placode-derived TrkB and TrkC neurons show no defects in Elp1 CKO at examined stages, and the placode-derived geniculate ganglion shows no perturbations. A placode-targeted deletion of Elp1 would likely affect TrkB neurons based on expression patterns and studies in epibranchial ganglia.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C153 state observations from the current study showing no effects on placode-derived neurons in the neural crest-specific knockout. Claim C154 cites a recent study on epibranchial ganglia. Claims C155-C156 are speculative predictions about what would happen with a placode-specific deletion, appropriately framed as speculation and based on reasonable extrapolation from Elp1 expression patterns and cited studies.

results.result: Innervation of the whisker pad is initiated by E11.5 in both Control and Elp1 CKO, but the innervation field does not expand substantially in Elp1 CKO. Early maxillary nerve fibers at E11 express predominantly TrkB or TrkC, suggesting placode-derived neurons may reach targets first and act as scaffolds for later TrkA axons.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C158 are supported by whole-mount imaging data (Figures 3-5). Claim C160 provides immunohistochemistry data showing the predominance of TrkB/TrkC in early maxillary nerve fibers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Claim C159 is a speculative interpretation but is reasonable given the temporal sequence of TrkB/TrkC versus TrkA neurogenesis and the observation that some innervation occurs in Elp1 CKO despite TrkA deficits.

results.result: The Wnt1-Cre driver targets approximately 90% of Sox10-positive neural crest cells in the trigeminal ganglion, similar to previous reports in the trunk. While a population of non-recombined neural crest derivatives remains, Wnt1-Cre is commonly used and achieves more efficient recombination than other drivers like Sox10-Cre.
results.evaluation: Claim C162 provides quantitative data (92.1% recombination efficiency) supported by Figure 7 and cited comparison to trunk studies. Claims C161 and C163 acknowledge the limitation of incomplete recombination. Claims C164-C165 cite previous literature justifying the use of Wnt1-Cre despite this limitation. This is an appropriate discussion of experimental limitations and validation of the approach.

results.result: Elp1 CKO phenotypes are more extreme than human FD due to complete loss of Elp1 from neural crest derivatives, whereas FD patients retain some Elp1 protein. It is unclear whether certain neuronal subpopulations are more affected in FD patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C167 appropriately compare the mouse model to human disease, citing the molecular basis of FD (Slaugenhaupt et al., 2001). Claim C168 acknowledges a knowledge gap in understanding cellular-level effects in human patients. This is an appropriate discussion of model limitations and translational considerations.
